say.text: A 48-year-old has a single 3 cm invasive ductal cancer in a large breast. No distant spread.
Which operation do you plan for the breast?

choices.label: Halsted radical mastectomy, the most complete clearance
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about what each operation removes, and what survival data show for keeping the breast.
That is not the right choice.
Halsted looks thorough and was the textbook operation, but it removes both pectoral muscles and the whole axilla, and it is now rarely done.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Old keys still teach Halsted as the standard, so check what current practice uses before you trust that memory.

say.text: Yes. In a suitable early cancer, breast conservation with whole-breast radiotherapy gives survival equal to mastectomy.
If conservation is not suitable, the modern option is modified radical mastectomy, which keeps pectoralis major.
Suppose a mastectomy is needed, and the surgeon picks modified radical over Halsted. Why?

choices.label: It keeps pectoralis major and still clears the axilla
Removing both pectoral muscles makes the cure complete
It clears the axilla first, so staging is not needed
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what each operation takes away from the chest wall, and which of those losses the patient does not need.
That is not the right choice.
More muscle removal feels like extra safety, but Halsted takes pectoralis major and minor and all three axillary levels, and that extra loss is not what makes a mastectomy curative.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the logic: more removal is not the same as more cure. Re-read what Halsted removes.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Clearing nodes is part of a mastectomy, but dissection does not replace staging, and the axilla is staged by its own test first.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two decisions: which operation, and how the axilla is staged.

say.text: Yes. Modified radical mastectomy removes the breast and the axillary nodes, but keeps pectoralis major, so the chest wall loses less.
Which of these is a true contraindication to breast-conserving surgery?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: A contraindication stops clear margins or safe radiotherapy. Which option does that?
Yes. Tumour in separate quadrants, or diffuse suspicious calcification, cannot be cleared through one conserved breast.
That is not the right choice.
Five centimetres is a number people remember, so size feels like a cut-off; but size matters only relative to the breast and to cosmesis.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The list is built from what stops clear margins or safe radiotherapy, not from one size number.

say.text: A 6 cm tumour in a moderate breast shrinks to 2 cm after neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
Can breast conservation still be offered?

choices.label: No, a tumour above 5 cm forbids it
Yes, with whole-breast radiotherapy after surgery
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Check the size after treatment, not before, and ask whether the breast can still give clear margins.
That is not the right choice.
The 5 cm figure tempts as a fixed rule, but the question is whether the tumour can be cleared, and shrinkage after treatment changes that.

sure_note.text: You were sure. A fixed number carried over from the staging list is the mistake; check the size now, against the breast.

say.text: Yes. Downstaging does not block conservation, provided clear margins can be achieved. Whole-breast radiotherapy is still given after the operation.
A 50-year-old has a 2 cm invasive ductal cancer and a clinically node-negative axilla.
What is the first axillary procedure?

choices.label: Sentinel lymph node biopsy to stage the axilla
Level I and II axillary dissection, done first
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the axilla needs first: a test to stage it, or a clearance before anyone knows its status.
Yes. For a clinically node-negative invasive cancer, sentinel node biopsy is the standard staging, using radioisotope and/or blue dye.
That is not the right choice.
Clearance looks thorough, so it seems to come first; but it removes levels I and II before anyone has tested the nodes.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recheck the order: what the axilla needs first, and what a positive test would change.

say.text: Patient A is node-negative on examination. Patient B has a biopsy-proven node-positive axilla.
What is the plan for each?

choices.label: A gets SLNB; B goes to ALND
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what each axilla still needs: a test to stage it, or a clearance because nodes are already involved.
That is not the right choice.
Full dissection feels thorough for both, but for a clinically negative axilla it adds arm morbidity that a sentinel biopsy avoids.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two patients: node status alone decides the axillary plan.

say.text: Yes. A node-negative axilla is staged by sentinel node biopsy. A biopsy-proven positive axilla goes to dissection, and sentinel biopsy is not used there.
Which nerve is most commonly injured in axillary lymph node dissection?

choices.label: Long thoracic nerve, the one that causes winging
Intercostobrachial nerve, the one that is often sacrificed
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about which nerve runs through the axilla, and which deficit is most common after a clearance.
Yes. The intercostobrachial nerve is the one most often sacrificed, and its loss numbs the medial upper arm.
That is not the right choice.
Winging is the dramatic deficit, so it feels like the common one; but long thoracic injury paralyses serratus anterior and is not the nerve most often hit.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate frequency from drama: the nerve that causes winging is not the one most often injured.

say.text: After axillary dissection, a patient has numbness of the medial upper arm and no winging of the scapula.
What explains this?

choices.label: Long thoracic nerve injured, the commonest nerve injury
Intercostobrachial nerve sacrificed, the commonest nerve injury
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Match the two symptoms to the two nerves, then ask which of those nerves is also the most often injured.
That is not the right choice.
A dramatic deficit feels frequent, but winging is the long thoracic pattern, and this patient has no winging.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pin the deficit to its nerve first, then ask which injury is commonest.

say.text: Yes. Numbness of the medial upper arm points to the intercostobrachial nerve, and that is also the commonest nerve injury.
Winging would have pointed to the long thoracic nerve, which supplies serratus anterior.
